  Equity Impact Statement
  The County of San Diego (County) housing initiatives continue to prioritize low‑income
  households, seniors, people with disabilities, and residents at risk of and experiencing
  homelessness by expanding access to stable, affordable housing. Through focused investments,
  tenant protections, homeownership support, and the use of public land for affordable housing,
  the County seeks to reduce disparities and strengthen opportunities for historically underserved
  communities. By focusing on expanding housing options at various income levels, preserving
  vulnerable housing, and preventing displacement, these initiatives help ensure all residents,

Wednesday, October 7, 2026  4
   regardless of race, income, age, or geography, can live in safe, healthy, and thriving
  communities.

  Sustainability Impact Statement
  Today’s actions support the County of San Diego’s (County) Sustainability Goal #2 to provide
  just and equitable access and Sustainability Goal #4 to protect health and well-being for
  residents. The County’s housing efforts support sustainability by promoting compact, resilient,
  and efficient development patterns aligned with the County’s broader climate, land use, and
  sustainability goals. Investments in affordable housing create long-term housing opportunities,
  reduce displacement, and strengthen neighborhoods. Additionally, affordable housing
  contributes to community sustainability by providing stable living environments that support
  health, safety, and wellbeing. Ensuring affordable housing developments are restricted to
  vulnerable populations including lower-income households, persons experiencing homelessness,
  seniors, and veterans also reduces economic disparities and promotes equitable communities.
  These initiatives collectively advance the County’s sustainability goals by integrating
  environmental, economic, and social considerations into housing policy and development.

  Fiscal Impact
  Recommendations 1-4
  There is no fiscal impact associated with today’s recommendation for the Board to receive the
  Housing Workshop presentation and Innovative Housing Trust Fund 5-year report back. There
  will be no change in net General Fund costs and no additional staff years.

  Recommendation 5
  There is no fiscal impact associated with this recommendation. There may be future fiscal
  impacts based on recommendations from today’s action. If this recommendation is approved,
  this may result in future annual costs up to $3 million which ($2.9 million for Tenant Legal
  Services and $0.1 million for Fair Housing Program) in FY 2028-29, subject to available
  funding. It is estimated that there could be total costs of up to $15 million from FY 2028-29
  through FY 2032-33, subject to available funding. There is available ongoing General Purpose
  Revenue of $1.5 million annually allocated to the Tenant Legal Services and Fair Housing
  programs. To fund the full $3 million future costs, $1.5 million in additional funding will need
  to be identified and will proceed once determined. Funds for subsequent years will be
  incorporated into future operational plans. At this time, there will be no change in net General
  Fund cost and no additional staff years.

  Background
  San Diego County continues to experience a significant housing shortage and affordability
  challenge that affects households throughout the region. The limited supply of housing, coupled
  with rising development costs and increasing prices, has made it difficult for many residents to
  obtain and maintain stable housing. Housing production rates in the region have not kept pace

Wednesday, October 7, 2026  5
   with the population growth and demand for extremely low and very low-income housing. These
  challenges contribute to housing instability and increase the risk of homelessness, especially for
  vulnerable populations including low-income households, seniors, veterans, and individuals with
  disabilities. Addressing this crisis requires shared responsibility and tremendous collaboration
  among private industry, nonprofit organizations, and other local governments throughout the
  region.

  In response to the housing crisis, the San Diego County Board of Supervisors (Board) has
  strengthened the County of San Diego’s (County) role by directing initiatives that invest in
  housing preservation, promote housing stability, and address barriers to housing access and
  production. The Board adopted five overarching housing goals, known as the 5 Ps within the
  County’s vision of a just, sustainable, and resilient future for all: Promote Equity, Inclusion, and
  Sustainability; Produce Housing for All; Preserve Vulnerable Housing; Protect Tenants; and
  Prevent Displacement. The five goals provide a roadmap to expand affordable housing options,
  keep more people in their homes, improve efficiency, streamline processes, and strengthen
  engagement with the community. Recognizing the immense need for affordable housing and
  housing stability across the region, the County has a vision of Housing for All, focused on
  making tangible progress on the Board’s adopted housing goals.

  Housing for All Initiative
  The Housing for All Initiative addresses the County’s housing shortage through a comprehensive
  framework guided by the 5 Ps focusing on equity, housing production, vulnerable housing
  preservation, tenant protection, and displacement prevention. This initiative is not a new
  approach, but rather a unification of our existing housing initiatives, frameworks, and strategies
  under one coherent identity. To improve consistency, “Housing for All Initiative” will be used as
  the primary term to describe the County’s housing efforts. This shift in alignment demonstrates
  the County’s dedication to a unified, long-term strategy for expanding housing opportunities and
  strengthening stability for residents.

  On December 13, 2022 (30), the Board held the Let’s Talk Housing Workshop to address the
  housing crisis. The workshop focused on the County’s overarching housing goals and the need
  for a strategy that can achieve these priorities within existing and future resources. As a result of
  the workshop, on August 27, 2024 (14), the Board received the Housing Blueprint (Blueprint), a
  comprehensive roadmap intended to address the root causes of the housing crisis in the San
  Diego region. Organized around the 5 Ps, the Blueprint identifies eight strategies that guide
  implementation of the Housing for All Initiative and align housing investments, land-use tools,
  and community engagement. Additionally, on November 19, 2025 (1), the Board received the
  Housing Forward presentation with updates on housing policy and production in the
  unincorporated areas of the county. At that workshop, the Board and stakeholders emphasized
  aligning zoning with the General Plan, focusing housing in villages and infill areas, protecting
  existing homes and renters, and working with cities on regional housing needs. The Board also
  discussed innovative housing models and a potential VMT mitigation pathway for projects that
  cannot use existing CEQA streamlining.

  To prioritize Blueprint actions, County subject matter experts and leaders across the enterprise
  developed an implementation plan that aligns the Blueprint goals and strategies with ongoing
  County initiatives. On May 15, 2025, the Board received a memorandum regarding the
  implementation of the Housing Blueprint. The memorandum included a Housing Blueprint
  Implementation Action Plan, which has since been updated to summarize actions undertaken and
  implementation progress made by County departments in support of the broader Housing for All
  Initiative. The purpose of today’s workshop is to highlight these efforts and request that the
  Board adopt the Housing for All Initiative as the County’s overarching housing framework.

  Housing for All Implementation Progress
  The Board has guided efforts to address the housing crisis by directing initiatives that address
  barriers to accessing and producing housing. The County has taken a leadership role in
  advancing innovative, coordinated, and impactful housing solutions. Recognizing that
  addressing the housing crisis and carrying out the Blueprint’s actions requires a comprehensive
  approach, County departments continue to work collaboratively to align resources, expertise, and
  programs that support housing production, preservation, and stability. Through ongoing
  interdepartmental coordination, departments such as Housing and Community Development
  Services (HCDS), Planning & Development Services (PDS), and the Department of General
  Services (DGS) are identifying opportunities to streamline processes, leverage funding, address
  barriers to housing development, and connect residents to critical housing and supportive
  services. This collaborative approach strengthens the County’s ability to advance meaningful
  progress toward the Board’s housing goals, ensuring that all residents have access to safe, stable,
  and affordable housing.

  Innovative Housing Trust Fund Update

Wednesday, October 7, 2026  9
   The development and preservation of multifamily affordable housing remain a critical
  component of addressing the region’s housing needs. Through strategic investments and
  partnerships, HHSA has supported developments that increase the availability of safe, stable,
  and affordable housing for families, seniors, veterans, and individuals at risk of or experiencing
  homelessness.

  One of the key factors strengthening the development of affordable multifamily housing across
  the region is the Board-initiated Innovative Housing Trust Fund (IHTF). On October 10, 2017
  (7), the Board established the IHTF to address affordable housing needs throughout San Diego
  County with the direction that staff provide an update on the IHTF every five years. Today’s
  update serves as the update for 2022-2027. Prior to 2017, HHSA’s investment in affordable
  housing totaled $55 million over a span of 35 years. Since the creation of the IHTF, HHSA has
  invested over $330 million in local, State, and federal sources for the construction of affordable
  housing across San Diego County. This investment, along with the use of excess County-owned
  land, has leveraged over $3 billion and will create 6,045 deed-restricted housing units in 72
  affordable housing developments throughout the region.

  Since 2017, the Board has allocated over $129 million to the IHTF through seven funding
  allocations. To date, $112 million in IHTF funds and accrued interest has been awarded to 36
  affordable housing developments across 22 communities throughout the region, representing a
  portion of the $330 million invested in local communities. These funds leveraged $1.6 billion in
  public and private funding to support construction of 36 developments. Once completed, 3,054
  deed-restricted housing units will become homes to approximately 6,700 low-income
  households, providing long-term safe, sustainable housing. At this time, 2,217 units have
  completed construction, 318 units are under construction, and 519 units will be constructed
  and/or rehabilitated within the next one to four years (see Attachment C for IHTF development
  summary). Staff anticipate awarding the most recent allocation of $22 million to development
  partners through NOFAs in FY 2026-27. Following award of IHTF funding, construction may
  begin at the development sites within the next two to four years. Per the San Diego County Code
  of Administrative Ordinances, this report serves as the five-year report back to the Board on
  IHTF.

  Looking Ahead/Future Priorities
  While meaningful progress has been made, the need for affordable housing continues to grow.
  The County remains committed to advancing the Housing for All Initiative by supporting
  innovative housing solutions, strengthening partnerships, and pursuing new opportunities that
  expand access to affordable housing.

  Partnerships and inter-departmental collaboration are key to advancing housing solutions,
  exemplified by the County’s support for three developments on faith-based land that will
  provide 220 affordable units, with doors opening in the next one to four years. In addition, the
  County’s internal partnerships are instrumental in maximizing public benefit and advancing
  community housing goals. La Sábila, an affordable housing development in unincorporated
  Vista, is one example of this approach, bringing together several County departments and the
  mission-driven non-profit developer, Wakeland Housing and Development Corporation, to
  provide 85-units for low-income and formerly homeless seniors. This effort reduced duplication,
  improved efficiency, and ensured a full-spectrum approach to housing needs in our communities.

Wednesday, October 7, 2026  10
   Collaboration with other local jurisdictions is another key component of advancing the region’s
  shared housing goals, such as the October 2022 joint City of San Diego/County resolution to
  formally express the intent to “take joint action to increase the availability of affordable
  housing” in the region. This resolution formalized the City of San Diego and the County’s intent
  to support efforts to build 10,000 affordable units on government-owned land by 2030, leverage
  public/private funding, and support the streamlining of permitting affordable housing. Through
  both direct partnerships and individual jurisdiction-led efforts, our shared housing goals have
  helped advance a total of 6,917 units opened, under construction, or planned across the region on
  public land as of March 2026, with more work ahead to reach our goal of 10,000 units.

  In addition, funding is the foundation of every successful housing initiative. Moving forward,
  identifying a dedicated revenue stream for the Innovative Housing Trust Fund will ensure the
  long-term sustainability of affordable housing development. An ongoing source of local funding
  would provide the flexibility needed to advance new housing options while allowing the County
  to leverage State and federal funding resources. By creating a sustainable local investment, the
  County can maximize external resources, accelerate affordable housing development, and help
  address the region’s long-term housing needs. Ongoing dedicated funding for the IHTF aids the
  County’s housing goal to plan multi-year development pipelines, preserve existing affordable
  homes, and invest in programs that keep residents stably housed.

  Competitive Solicitation for Tenant Legal Services and Fair Housing Program
  The County will continue to invest in programs and services that provide critical support to
  households facing housing instability and affordability challenges. This is evident in the
  administration of the Tenant Legal Services and Fair Housing programs through partnerships
  with Legal Aid Society of San Diego, the University of San Diego, and CSA San Diego to
  streamline referrals between community partners providing tenant legal services. The County’s
  Tenant Legal Services and Fair Housing programs play a key role in protecting tenants by
  providing critical legal assistance to those who are facing eviction or other housing challenges.

  On July 13, 2021 (7), the Board of Supervisors (Board) approved a competitive solicitation for
  legal services, housing counseling, prevention, and outreach activities. As a result, contract
  567549 was awarded to Legal Aid Society of San Diego, set to end on June 30, 2028. Through a
  combination of legal counseling, outreach, education, and eviction prevention services, the
  program has focused on reaching vulnerable and underserved populations, helping residents
  understand their rights, navigate complex legal processes, and gain access to resources they may
  not otherwise be able to obtain. In calendar year 2025, the program served 2,346 clients. The
  County’s investment in the Tenant Legal Services reflects its commitment to stabilizing
  residents in their homes, preventing homelessness, and promoting long-term community
  well-being.

  On April 5, 2022 (3), the Board of Supervisors approved the competitive solicitation of the
  County’s Fair Housing Program which protects people from discrimination when renting or
  buying a home, getting a mortgage, seeking housing assistance, or engaging in other
  housing-related activities. As a result, Contract 570062 was awarded to CSA San Diego County
  with an annual County investment of $100,000 for one year and an option to extend for four
  years. In Fiscal Year 2025-26, the program hosted 12 public seminars, published 12 articles,

Wednesday, October 7, 2026  11
   provided 16 hours of on-site/on-demand training, and conducted 40 fair housing tests to
  landlords, tenants, and housing contractors. Contract 570062 is set to end on June 30, 2028.

  Both contracts end dates will be aligned for these critical programs, and allow for one
  competitive solicitation for both services. Aligning the contract timelines and combining the
  services into a single solicitation will streamline administrative efforts and enhance coordination
  to better support tenant protection and address housing discrimination throughout the region.
  Additionally, the competitive solicitation for these services will align with the County’s
  commitment to strengthening opportunities for small and local businesses.

  Today’s action asks the Board to receive the Housing Workshop and formally adopt the Housing
  for All Initiative as the County’s overarching housing framework for current and future housing
  efforts. Additional actions before the Board include accepting this update to comply with the
  Innovative Housing Trust Fund five-year report back, and authorize the release of a competitive
  solicitation for Tenant Legal Services and Fair Housing programs to streamline tenant protection
  efforts and improve service efficiency. These efforts reflect the County’s commitment to
  equitable and sustainable housing solutions that enhance stability and opportunity for residents,
  while setting the stage for future policy discussions and Board actions to strengthen partnerships
  and advance long‑term housing affordability and resilience.

  Linkage To The County Of San Diego Strategic Plan
  Today’s action supports the County of San Diego 2026-31 Strategic Plan Initiatives of
  Sustainability (Economy and Resiliency), Equity (Housing and Economic Opportunity), and
  Community (Engagement, Quality of Life, and Partnership). Additionally, today’s actions
  support the regional Live Well San Diego vision of healthy, safe, and thriving communities and
  the Housing for All Initiative by supporting the development of safe and affordable housing for
  low-income households and improving the housing and service delivery system for individuals
  at risk of experiencing homelessness through collaborative solutions.

  Respectfully submitted,

  When the Board of Supervisors meets as the governing body of a special district, they are acting

  decisions that apply only to that specific district, such as approving its budgets, projects,
  policies, and operations. These actions are legally separate from the Board’s actions as the
  County of San Diego, and they apply only to the area and responsibilities of the special district.

  Equity Impact Statement
  The County of San Diego (County) housing initiatives continue to prioritize low‑income
  households, seniors, people with disabilities, and residents at risk of and experiencing
  homelessness by expanding access to stable, affordable housing. Through focused investments,
  tenant protections, homeownership support, and the use of public land for affordable housing, the
  County seeks to reduce disparities and strengthen opportunities for historically underserved
  communities. By focusing on expanding housing options at various income levels, preserving
  vulnerable housing, and preventing displacement, these initiatives help ensure all residents,
  regardless of race, income, age, or geography, can live in safe, healthy, and thriving
  communities.

  Sustainability Impact Statement
  Today’s actions support the County of San Diego’s (County) Sustainability Goal #2 to provide
  just and equitable access and Sustainability Goal #4 to protect health and well-being for
  residents. The County’s housing efforts support sustainability by promoting compact, resilient,
  and efficient development patterns aligned with the County’s broader climate, land use, and
  sustainability goals. Investments in affordable housing create long-term housing opportunities,
  reduce displacement, and strengthen neighborhoods. Additionally, affordable housing contributes
  to community sustainability by providing stable living environments that support health, safety,
  and wellbeing. Ensuring affordable housing developments are restricted to vulnerable
  populations including lower-income households, persons experiencing homelessness, seniors,
  and veterans also reduces economic disparities and promotes equitable communities. These

   initiatives collectively advance the County’s sustainability goals by integrating environmental,
  economic, and social considerations into housing policy and development.

  Background
  San Diego County continues to experience a significant housing shortage and affordability
  challenge that affects households throughout the region. The limited supply of housing, coupled
  with rising development costs and increasing prices, has made it difficult for many residents to
  obtain and maintain stable housing. Housing production rates in the region have not kept pace
  with the population growth and demand for extremely low and very low-income housing. These
  challenges contribute to housing instability and increase the risk of homelessness, especially for
  vulnerable populations including low-income households, seniors, veterans, and individuals with
  disabilities. Addressing this crisis requires shared responsibility and tremendous collaboration
  among private industry, nonprofit organizations, and other local governments throughout the
  region.

  In response to the housing crisis, the San Diego County Board of Supervisors (Board) has
  strengthened the County of San Diego’s (County) role by directing initiatives that invest in
  housing preservation, promote housing stability, and address barriers to housing access and
  production. The Board adopted five overarching housing goals, known as the 5 Ps within the
  County’s vision of a just, sustainable, and resilient future for all: Promote Equity, Inclusion, and
  Sustainability; Produce Housing for All; Preserve Vulnerable Housing; Protect Tenants; and
  Prevent Displacement. The five goals provide a roadmap to expand affordable housing options,
  keep more people in their homes, improve efficiency, streamline processes, and strengthen

WEDNESDAY, OCTOBER 7, 2026  5
   engagement with the community. Recognizing the immense need for affordable housing and
  housing stability across the region, the County has a vision of Housing for All, focused on
  making tangible progress on the Board’s adopted housing goals.

  Housing for All Initiative
  The Housing for All Initiative addresses the County’s housing shortage through a comprehensive
  framework guided by the 5 Ps focusing on equity, housing production, vulnerable housing
  preservation, tenant protection, and displacement prevention. This initiative is not a new
  approach, but rather a unification of our existing housing initiatives, frameworks, and strategies
  under one coherent identity. To improve consistency, “Housing for All Initiative” will be used as
  the primary term to describe the County’s housing efforts. This shift in alignment demonstrates
  the County’s dedication to a unified, long-term strategy for expanding housing opportunities and
  strengthening stability for residents.

  On December 13, 2022 (30), the Board held the Let’s Talk Housing Workshop to address the
  housing crisis. The workshop focused on the County’s overarching housing goals and the need
  for a strategy that can achieve these priorities within existing and future resources. As a result of
  the workshop, on August 27, 2024 (14), the Board received the Housing Blueprint (Blueprint), a
  comprehensive roadmap intended to address the root causes of the housing crisis in the San
  Diego region. Organized around the 5 Ps, the Blueprint identifies eight strategies that guide
  implementation of the Housing for All Initiative and align housing investments, land-use tools,
  and community engagement. Additionally, on November 19, 2025 (1), the Board received the
  Housing Forward presentation with updates on housing policy and production in the
  unincorporated areas of the county. At that workshop, the Board and stakeholders emphasized
  aligning zoning with the General Plan, focusing housing in villages and infill areas, protecting
  existing homes and renters, and working with cities on regional housing needs. The Board also
  discussed innovative housing models and a potential VMT mitigation pathway for projects that
  cannot use existing CEQA streamlining.

  Production and Programs 7) Implement Affordable Housing Preservation Strategies 8)

  To prioritize Blueprint actions, County subject matter experts and leaders across the enterprise
  developed an implementation plan that aligns the Blueprint goals and strategies with ongoing
  County initiatives. On May 15, 2025, the Board received a memorandum regarding the
  implementation of the Housing Blueprint. The memorandum included a Housing Blueprint
  Implementation Action Plan, which has since been updated to summarize actions undertaken and
  implementation progress made by County departments in support of the broader Housing for All
  Initiative. The purpose of today’s workshop is to highlight these efforts and request that the

  Housing for All Implementation Progress
  The Board has guided efforts to address the housing crisis by directing initiatives that address
  barriers to accessing and producing housing. The County has taken a leadership role in advancing
  innovative, coordinated, and impactful housing solutions. Recognizing that addressing the
  housing crisis and carrying out the Blueprint’s actions requires a comprehensive approach,
  County departments continue to work collaboratively to align resources, expertise, and programs
  that support housing production, preservation, and stability. Through ongoing interdepartmental
  coordination, departments such as Housing and Community Development Services (HCDS),
  Planning & Development Services (PDS), and the Department of General Services (DGS) are
  identifying opportunities to streamline processes, leverage funding, address barriers to housing
  development, and connect residents to critical housing and supportive services. This
  collaborative approach strengthens the County’s ability to advance meaningful progress toward
  the Board’s housing goals, ensuring that all residents have access to safe, stable, and affordable
  housing.

  Innovative Housing Trust Fund Update

  component of addressing the region’s housing needs. Through strategic investments and
  partnerships, HHSA has supported developments that increase the availability of safe, stable, and
  affordable housing for families, seniors, veterans, and individuals at risk of or experiencing
  homelessness.

  One of the key factors strengthening the development of affordable multifamily housing across
  the region is the Board-initiated Innovative Housing Trust Fund (IHTF). On October 10, 2017
  (7), the Board established the IHTF to address affordable housing needs throughout San Diego
  County with the direction that staff provide an update on the IHTF every five years. Today’s
  update serves as the update for 2022-2027. Prior to 2017, HHSA’s investment in affordable
  housing totaled $55 million over a span of 35 years. Since the creation of the IHTF, HHSA has
  invested over $330 million in local, State, and federal sources for the construction of affordable
  housing across San Diego County. This investment, along with the use of excess County-owned
  land, has leveraged over $3 billion and will create 6,045 deed-restricted housing units in 72
  affordable housing developments throughout the region.

  Since 2017, the Board has allocated over $129 million to the IHTF through seven funding

   allocations. To date, $112 million in IHTF funds and accrued interest has been awarded to 36
  affordable housing developments across 22 communities throughout the region, representing a
  portion of the $330 million invested in local communities. These funds leveraged $1.6 billion in
  public and private funding to support construction of 36 developments. Once completed, 3,054
  deed-restricted housing units will become homes to approximately 6,700 low-income
  households, providing long-term safe, sustainable housing. At this time, 2,217 units have
  completed construction, 318 units are under construction, and 519 units will be constructed
  and/or rehabilitated within the next one to four years (see Attachment C for IHTF development
  summary). Staff anticipate awarding the most recent allocation of $22 million to development
  partners through NOFAs in FY 2026-27. Following award of IHTF funding, construction may
  begin at the development sites within the next two to four years. Per the San Diego County Code
  of Administrative Ordinances, this report serves as the five-year report back to the Board on
  IHTF.

  Looking Ahead/Future Priorities
  While meaningful progress has been made, the need for affordable housing continues to grow.
  The County remains committed to advancing the Housing for All Initiative by supporting
  innovative housing solutions, strengthening partnerships, and pursuing new opportunities that
  expand access to affordable housing.

  Partnerships and inter-departmental collaboration are key to advancing housing solutions,
  exemplified by the County’s support for three developments on faith-based land that will provide
  220 affordable units, with doors opening in the next one to four years. In addition, the County’s
  internal partnerships are instrumental in maximizing public benefit and advancing community
  housing goals. La Sábila, an affordable housing development in unincorporated Vista, is one
  example of this approach, bringing together several County departments and the mission-driven
  non-profit developer, Wakeland Housing and Development Corporation, to provide 85-units for
  low-income and formerly homeless seniors. This effort reduced duplication, improved efficiency,
  and ensured a full-spectrum approach to housing needs in our communities.

  Collaboration with other local jurisdictions is another key component of advancing the region’s
  shared housing goals, such as the October 2022 joint City of San Diego/County resolution to
  formally express the intent to “take joint action to increase the availability of affordable
  housing” in the region. This resolution formalized the City of San Diego and the County’s intent
  to support efforts to build 10,000 affordable units on government-owned land by 2030, leverage
  public/private funding, and support the streamlining of permitting affordable housing. Through
  both direct partnerships and individual jurisdiction-led efforts, our shared housing goals have
  helped advance a total of 6,917 units opened, under construction, or planned across the region on
  public land as of March 2026, with more work ahead to reach our goal of 10,000 units.

  In addition, funding is the foundation of every successful housing initiative. Moving forward,
  identifying a dedicated revenue stream for the Innovative Housing Trust Fund will ensure the
  long-term sustainability of affordable housing development. An ongoing source of local funding
  would provide the flexibility needed to advance new housing options while allowing the County
  to leverage State and federal funding resources. By creating a sustainable local investment, the
  County can maximize external resources, accelerate affordable housing development, and help
  address the region’s long-term housing needs. Ongoing dedicated funding for the IHTF aids the
  County’s housing goal to plan multi-year development pipelines, preserve existing affordable

  Competitive Solicitation for Tenant Legal Services and Fair Housing Program
  The County will continue to invest in programs and services that provide critical support to
  households facing housing instability and affordability challenges. This is evident in the
  administration of the Tenant Legal Services and Fair Housing programs through partnerships
  with Legal Aid Society of San Diego, the University of San Diego, and CSA San Diego to
  streamline referrals between community partners providing tenant legal services. The County’s
  Tenant Legal Services and Fair Housing programs play a key role in protecting tenants by
  providing critical legal assistance to those who are facing eviction or other housing challenges.

  On July 13, 2021 (7), the Board of Supervisors (Board) approved a competitive solicitation for
  legal services, housing counseling, prevention, and outreach activities. As a result, contract
  567549 was awarded to Legal Aid Society of San Diego, set to end on June 30, 2028. Through a
  combination of legal counseling, outreach, education, and eviction prevention services, the
  program has focused on reaching vulnerable and underserved populations, helping residents
  understand their rights, navigate complex legal processes, and gain access to resources they may
  not otherwise be able to obtain. In calendar year 2025, the program served 2,346 clients. The
  County’s investment in the Tenant Legal Services reflects its commitment to stabilizing residents
  in their homes, preventing homelessness, and promoting long-term community well-being.

  On April 5, 2022 (3), the Board of Supervisors approved the competitive solicitation of the
  County’s Fair Housing Program which protects people from discrimination when renting or
  buying a home, getting a mortgage, seeking housing assistance, or engaging in other
  housing-related activities. As a result, Contract 570062 was awarded to CSA San Diego County
  with an annual County investment of $100,000 for one year and an option to extend for four
  years. In Fiscal Year 2025-26, the program hosted 12 public seminars, published 12 articles,
  provided 16 hours of on-site/on-demand training, and conducted 40 fair housing tests to
  landlords, tenants, and housing contractors. Contract 570062 is set to end on June 30, 2028.

  Both contracts end dates will be aligned for these critical programs, and allow for one
  competitive solicitation for both services. Aligning the contract timelines and combining the
  services into a single solicitation will streamline administrative efforts and enhance coordination
  to better support tenant protection and address housing discrimination throughout the region.
  Additionally, the competitive solicitation for these services will align with the County’s
  commitment to strengthening opportunities for small and local businesses.

  Today’s action asks the Board to receive the Housing Workshop and formally adopt the Housing
  for All Initiative as the County’s overarching housing framework for current and future housing
  efforts. Additional actions before the Board include accepting this update to comply with the
  Innovative Housing Trust Fund five-year report back, and authorize the release of a competitive
  solicitation for Tenant Legal Services and Fair Housing programs to streamline tenant protection
  efforts and improve service efficiency. These efforts reflect the County’s commitment to
  equitable and sustainable housing solutions that enhance stability and opportunity for residents,
  while setting the stage for future policy discussions and Board actions to strengthen partnerships
  and advance long‑term housing affordability and resilience.
